paras: The lynching of Jerry Hamilton was the fatal beating of a Black man by disguised men near Mount Vernon, Montgomery County, Georgia, on the night of May 2, 1881. Ten local men were charged under the federal civil rights bill and bound over to a United States grand jury; no report of a trial was found.
According to the Savannah Morning News, Hamilton had "in some manner" made himself "obnoxious"; no offense was named.
A party of disguised men took Hamilton from his house, carried him some distance and beat him so badly that he died. The number of attackers and the place of the beating were not reported.

The next day a mass meeting of citizens passed resolutions condemning the crime. On a warrant from United States Commissioner Wade, a deputy marshal brought ten Montgomery County men to Savannah on June 14. With the prosecution's witnesses absent on two days, the accused were bound over in $2,000 each to await the federal grand jury in November. The principal witness was described as a Black woman, and the affiant as a Black man.

The Savannah Morning News headlined its report "A Cowardly Crime" but called the accused "the very last men to countenance such an outrage." It said there appeared to be no evidence against them and that the offense did not fall under the civil rights bill. Its follow-up said the affiant bore "a notorious character" and stressed the "great inconvenience" to the accused.
An Atlanta dispatch in the Chicago Tribune of June 18, headed "Violating the Civil-Rights Bill," repeated the "prominent citizens" language and said the men were "being tried."

The Savannah paper dated the attack to May 2, while the Atlanta dispatch placed it "four nights since" June 17. The local account is the stronger evidence, since it describes a mass meeting the next day and arrests made by June 14.

reader.title: Lynching of Jerry Hamilton
bases: A party of disguised or masked men took Jerry Hamilton from his house at night and beat him so badly that he died (A1, A3).

Hamilton died of a beating by 'a party of disguised men' acting without any authority (A1, A3); no number of attackers is given and the only stated motive is that he had 'rendered himself obnoxious' (A1), so the group size and the pretext are implied rather than stated.

The only independent account is the Savannah Morning News (A1, A2); the Atlanta wire in the Chicago Tribune (A3) repeats its framing ('ten respectable citizens', 'obnoxious') and appears to derive from it, while differing on the date.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News (local)
accounts.gist: Disguised men took Hamilton from his house near Mount Vernon on the night of May 2, carried him some distance and beat him fatally; the paper condemned the crime but defended the ten accused as respectable men arrested on suspicion without evidence.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Masked men took Hamilton from home 'four nights since' and beat him to death; ten prominent Montgomery County citizens were being tried before Commissioner Wade at Savannah under the Civil Rights bill.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Cowardly Crime' but subheaded 'Ten Respectable Citizens Charged With a Serious Offense'; called the accused 'the very last men to countenance such an outrage', said there was no evidence against them and that the offense did not come under the civil rights bill.
'The Montgomery County Affair' discredited the Black affiant as of 'notorious character' and stressed the 'great inconvenience' to the accused and the neighbors who signed their bonds.
Ran as a brief, 'Violating the Civil-Rights Bill', among criminal news, with the 'obnoxious character' description and 'prominent citizens' language.

versions.value: 'four nights since' a June 17 dispatch (about June 13)

conflicts.note: The local Savannah report, which describes a mass meeting held the day after and an arrest process already completed by June 14, is the better evidence; the wire's 'four nights since' appears to be an error.

versions.value: Ten men; nine named: Joseph Palmer, William Adams, Thomas Norris, Angus Norris, Algernon Brady, R. Brady, H. Brady, W. Darley, James Buckan
Ten men; eight named: James Palmer, W. Adams, Thomas Morris, August Morris, Algernon Brady, Richard Brady, W. Darley, James Buchan
